sections.title: 1. Genesis of the Act: Lord Cornwallis's Preconditions

masteryZone.q: Which Governor-General was appointed in 1786, leading to the enactment of the Amending Act of 1786?
opts: Warren Hastings
Lord Cornwallis
Sir John Shore
Lord Wellesley
masteryZone.sol: Lord Cornwallis was appointed in 1786, and the Act was passed to meet his preconditions.

masteryZone.q: What was the main reason Cornwallis demanded override powers over his Council?
opts: He wanted to become a monarch.
He feared Council opposition leading to deadlock, as Warren Hastings had experienced.
He wished to annex Madras.
He wanted to abolish EIC trade.
masteryZone.sol: Cornwallis was aware of the severe conflicts between Warren Hastings and his Council and wanted to ensure administrative efficiency.

masteryZone.q: Which two offices were combined in Cornwallis under the 1786 Act?
opts: GG and Chief Justice
GG and Commander-in-Chief
Commander-in-Chief and President of Board of Control
GG and Governor of Bombay
masteryZone.sol: The offices of Governor-General of Bengal and Commander-in-Chief of British forces in India were combined.

masteryZone.q: Who was the Prime Minister of Great Britain in 1786 when this Act was passed?
opts: Lord North
William Pitt the Younger
Henry Dundas
George Grenville
masteryZone.sol: William Pitt the Younger was the Prime Minister.

masteryZone.q: Who acted as Governor-General in the interim between Warren Hastings and Lord Cornwallis?
opts: Sir John Shore
Sir John Macpherson
Lord Macartney
Lord Wellesley
masteryZone.sol: Sir John Macpherson officiated from 1785 to 1786.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following preconditions were demanded by Lord Cornwallis in 1786? (Select all that apply)
opts: Power to override the decision of his Council in special cases
Combining the offices of Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief
Abolition of the Board of Control
A permanent lifetime appointment as Governor-General
masteryZone.sol: Cornwallis demanded override power in special cases and unified civil-military command as Commander-in-Chief.

masteryZone.q: Which political figures in London supported Cornwallis's demands in 1786? (Select all that apply)
opts: William Pitt the Younger
Henry Dundas
Warren Hastings
Philip Francis
masteryZone.sol: Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger and Board of Control President Henry Dundas supported Cornwallis's demands.

masteryZone.q: What were the major challenges facing the EIC in 1786 that made Cornwallis's appointment urgent? (Select all that apply)
opts: Military threats from Tipu Sultan of Mysore
The need for land revenue reforms in Bengal
Administrative corruption inside the EIC
The loss of EIC's trade monopoly in China
masteryZone.sol: Mysore's military threat, need for revenue reform (which led to Permanent Settlement), and corruption were the key drivers. Monopoly in China was not lost until 1833.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following are true regarding Warren Hastings' Council conflicts that Cornwallis wanted to avoid? (Select all that apply)
opts: Hastings was frequently outvoted by Philip Francis and his allies.
Council standoffs paralyzed Hastings' foreign policy during wars.
Hastings had the power to override his Council but chose not to.
The conflicts led to Hastings' eventual impeachment in Parliament.
masteryZone.sol: Hastings did not have override power; he was frequently outvoted, paralyzing his administration and contributing to his impeachment.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following bodies in England participated in approving the special Act of 1786? (Select all that apply)
opts: The Court of Directors
The British Parliament
The Board of Control
The Supreme Court of Calcutta
masteryZone.sol: The Court of Directors, the British Parliament, and the Board of Control all concurred to make this special appointment. Supreme Court had no role in passing British acts.

masteryZone.q: Lord Cornwallis was a military general who had fought in the American Revolutionary War before coming to India.
masteryZone.sol: True. Lord Cornwallis was a British army general who surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.

masteryZone.q: Lord Cornwallis accepted the Governor-Generalship of Bengal immediately when it was first offered to him without any conditions.
masteryZone.sol: False. He refused to accept it unless his demands for override powers and military command were met.

masteryZone.q: Warren Hastings was in office as Governor-General when the Amending Act of 1786 was passed.
masteryZone.sol: False. Hastings left India in 1785. The Act was passed in 1786 to appoint Cornwallis.

masteryZone.q: The Touchet Committee recommended the combination of Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief offices.
masteryZone.sol: False. The Touchet Committee was associated with the Act of 1781, not 1786.

masteryZone.q: William Pitt the Younger opposed the concentration of civil and military power in Lord Cornwallis.
masteryZone.sol: False. Pitt supported Cornwallis and pushed the Amending Act of 1786 through Parliament.

masteryZone.q: The office of Commander-in-Chief was held by Warren Hastings during his entire tenure.
masteryZone.sol: False. The offices were separate and held by different individuals during Hastings' tenure.

masteryZone.q: The British cabinet wanted a strong executive in India to implement major land reforms and deal with regional military threats.
masteryZone.sol: True. This was the main administrative rationale for passing the Act of 1786.

masteryZone.q: Lord Cornwallis demanded the complete abolition of the Governor-General's Council in 1786.
masteryZone.sol: False. He wanted the power to override the Council in special cases, not to abolish it.

masteryZone.q: The Amending Act of 1786 was passed specifically to satisfy the preconditions of Lord ___________.
masteryZone.sol: The Act was passed to meet the demands of Lord Cornwallis.

masteryZone.q: Cornwallis demanded the power to override his Council in ___________ cases.
masteryZone.sol: He demanded override power in special/extraordinary cases, not routine ones.

masteryZone.q: The military office that Cornwallis demanded to be combined with the Governor-Generalship was that of ___________.
masteryZone.sol: He demanded the office of Commander-in-Chief.

masteryZone.q: The officiating Governor-General who served immediately before Cornwallis was Sir John ___________.
masteryZone.sol: Sir John Macpherson officiated from 1785 to 1786.

masteryZone.q: The British Prime Minister who supported Cornwallis's demands was William ___________.
masteryZone.sol: William Pitt the Younger supported Cornwallis's preconditions.

masteryZone.q: Warren ___________ experienced severe Council conflicts, which served as a warning to Cornwallis.
masteryZone.sol: Warren Hastings was frequently outvoted by his Council.

masteryZone.q: The President of the Board of Control who helped draft the Act of 1786 was Henry ___________.
masteryZone.sol: Henry Dundas drafted the terms of the Act.

masteryZone.q: The first major land reform Cornwallis wanted to execute with strong authority was the ___________ Settlement.
masteryZone.sol: The Permanent Settlement of land revenue was enacted in 1793.

masteryZone.q: Match the historical figures with their roles in the 1786 transition:

options.text: B. British Prime Minister who passed the Act
C. Board of Control President who drafted the Act

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match Cornwallis's demands with their corresponding administrative purposes:

options.text: A. Prevent council deadlocks and outvoting
B. Unify civil and military authority during war
C. Ensure stability to carry out land revenue reforms

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match the early acts of Company rule with the Council size they established:

options.text: C. Preserved 3 members but added GG override

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Whose preconditions directly led to the passing of the Amending Act of 1786?
masteryZone.sol: Lord Cornwallis's preconditions.

masteryZone.q: Which two offices were combined in a single person under the Act of 1786?
masteryZone.sol: The offices of Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief.

masteryZone.q: Name the Prime Minister of Great Britain in 1786.
masteryZone.sol: William Pitt the Younger.

masteryZone.q: Why did Cornwallis demand override power over his Council?
masteryZone.sol: To prevent Council deadlock and outvoting, which Warren Hastings had suffered.

masteryZone.q: Who officiated as Governor-General in the interim from 1785 to 1786?
masteryZone.sol: Sir John Macpherson.

masteryZone.q: Which board did Henry Dundas head when he assisted in passing the Act of 1786?
masteryZone.sol: The Board of Control.

masteryZone.q: What major land revenue reform was Cornwallis tasked to implement in Bengal?
masteryZone.sol: The Permanent Settlement of land revenue.

masteryZone.q: Did the Act of 1786 permanently merge the Commander-in-Chief office with the Governor-Generalship for all time?
masteryZone.sol: No, it only enabled them to be held by the same person if decided by EIC/Crown.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): Lord Cornwallis was appointed as both Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief in 1786.
Reason (R): He demanded unified civil-military command as a precondition to accept the post.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true, and R is the correct explanation.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): Warren Hastings supported the passing of the Amending Act of 1786.
Reason (R): Hastings wanted his successor to enjoy the same veto powers that he had during his tenure.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: A is false because Hastings was not in power and had no veto powers. R is false as Hastings never enjoyed veto powers.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The British Cabinet quickly passed the special Amending Act of 1786.
Reason (R): They were anxious to secure the services of Lord Cornwallis to reform Indian administration.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true, and R explains why they passed the Act.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): Sir John Macpherson was dismissed immediately in 1786.
Reason (R): The Act of 1786 abolished the office of officiating Governor-General.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are false. Macpherson was not dismissed but replaced, and the office was not abolished.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): Cornwallis demanded the power to override his Council.
Reason (R): He wanted to avoid the executive deadlock that Warren Hastings faced due to council opposition.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true and R is the correct explanation.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The office of Commander-in-Chief was permanently abolished in 1786.
Reason (R): Cornwallis wanted to eliminate all military influence from the EIC.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are false. The office was not abolished; it was combined with the GG.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): William Pitt the Younger drafted the Act of 1786.
Reason (R): Pitt wanted to weaken the Board of Control's influence in India.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: A is false (Henry Dundas drafted it under Pitt's cabinet). R is false (Pitt wanted to strengthen British control, not weaken Board of Control).

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): Cornwallis wanted sufficient authority to execute tax reforms.
Reason (R): Land revenue collection was critical for EIC finances and required a stable administration.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true, and R explains the need for stable authority for reforms.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the appointment of Lord Cornwallis:
1. He surrendered to American forces at Yorktown in 1781.
2. He accepted the Governor-Generalship in 1786 with the condition of holding military command.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct, describing Cornwallis's military background and his preconditions.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Warren Hastings suffered constant deadlocks with his Council.
2. Cornwallis demanded override power to prevent similar deadlocks.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct, explaining the genesis of the veto demand.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the British administration in 1786:
1. William Pitt the Younger was the Prime Minister.
2. Henry Dundas drafted the special Amending Act of 1786.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the officiating GG Sir John Macpherson:
1. He held office permanently from 1785 to 1793.
2. He was replaced by Lord Cornwallis in 1786.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is incorrect because he was only a temporary officiating Governor-General.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Cornwallis's preconditions:
1. He wanted to abolish the Board of Control.
2. He wanted to override his Council in special cases.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Statement 2 is correct. He did not want to abolish the Board of Control (Statement 1 is incorrect).

masteryZone.q: Why did Lord Cornwallis demand the power to override his Council?
masteryZone.sol: To prevent the administrative paralysis and constant outvoting that his predecessor Warren Hastings had faced, ensuring he could carry out necessary reforms efficiently.

masteryZone.q: Why did Cornwallis demand the office of Commander-in-Chief?
masteryZone.sol: To unify civil executive authority with supreme military command under a single head, preventing friction between the military and civil administration during campaigns.

masteryZone.q: Why did the British Parliament pass a special Amending Act in 1786 instead of waiting for a regular charter renewal?
masteryZone.sol: Because they were eager to secure Cornwallis's immediate services to stabilize Bengal and enact crucial land revenue reforms, requiring a quick statutory adjustment to satisfy his preconditions.

masteryZone.q: How did Warren Hastings' experience with his Council shape Cornwallis's demands?
masteryZone.sol: Hastings was frequently outvoted by his Council majority (Francis, Clavering, Monson), which paralyzed his administration. This served as a warning to Cornwallis, who refused the post unless granted a veto power.

masteryZone.q: How did William Pitt the Younger and Henry Dundas facilitate Cornwallis's appointment?
masteryZone.sol: By drafting and passing the Amending Act of 1786 in Parliament, which modified the existing laws to grant Cornwallis's demands.

masteryZone.q: How did the British public and Parliament view Cornwallis's preconditions?
masteryZone.sol: They viewed them as necessary concessions to secure a strong, incorruptible executive capable of stabilizing and reforming the EIC's administration in India.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: Philip Francis and other Council members constantly outvoted Warren Hastings on key policies. What does this case study show about the collegiate executive model established by the Regulating Act of 1773?
masteryZone.sol: It shows that a collective executive without a veto or override power leads to internal deadlock, administrative paralysis, and vulnerability in times of crisis.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: In 1786, the British Empire was recovering from the loss of the American colonies, and Cornwallis was a respected general. Why did the British Cabinet agree to Cornwallis's demands for concentrated power in India?
masteryZone.sol: To prevent another imperial loss, the Cabinet was willing to compromise on collegiate check-and-balance systems in favor of strong centralized executive control in the colonies.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: Before Cornwallis's arrival, EIC officials in Bengal were heavily involved in private trade and corruption. How did Cornwallis's preconditions help him clean up the administration?
masteryZone.sol: By giving him override power and command of the military, the preconditions provided him with the absolute authority needed to enforce strict rules and clean up corruption without fear of being blocked by self-interested councilors.

masteryZone.q: Explain the difference between the executive setups of Warren Hastings and Lord Cornwallis to a beginner.
masteryZone.sol: Hastings had no override power and was bound by the majority vote of his Council, leading to constant deadlocks. Cornwallis was granted the power to override his Council in special cases and combined it with military command, making him a much stronger, centralized executive.

masteryZone.q: Explain why the offices of Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief were combined in 1786.
masteryZone.sol: To ensure unified civil-military command, eliminating delays and conflicts between the army and civil administrators during wars with regional powers like Mysore.

masteryZone.q: Explain the significance of Lord Cornwallis's demands in British colonial history.
masteryZone.sol: His demands forced the British Parliament to pass a special act that concentrated civil and military powers, transitioning the colonial government from a collegiate system to a strong centralized executive presidency.

masteryZone.q: Under the Act of 1786, the Governor-General could override his council only in matters concerning:
opts: All trade and commerce
Ordinary revenue collection details
Safety, peace, or interests of the British presidency
Appeals of provincial civil courts
masteryZone.sol: The override veto was limited to extraordinary cases involving the safety, peace, or interests of EIC territories.

masteryZone.q: When the Governor-General overrode the Council, what was he required to do?
opts: Obtain the consent of the Chief Justice
Sign the orders personally and take sole responsibility
Suspend the dissenting members
Refer the case to a public vote
masteryZone.sol: He was required to sign the order himself, accepting complete personal accountability for the measures.

masteryZone.q: Which subsequent Act extended these override veto powers to all future Governor-Generals?
opts: Charter Act of 1793
Charter Act of 1813
Charter Act of 1833
Government of India Act 1858
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1793 extended this power to all future Governor-Generals and Presidency Governors.

masteryZone.q: The override power under the 1786 Act did NOT apply to which of the following?
opts: Military deployments
Judicial capacity when the GG-in-Council sat as Sadar Diwani Adalat
Foreign alliances
Peace treaty negotiations
masteryZone.sol: The veto was executive and administrative; it did not cover judicial capacity.

masteryZone.q: The Act of 1786 marked a constitutional shift from collaborative council government towards:
opts: Parliamentary democracy
A strong executive presidency model
Decentralized federalism
Absolute military dictatorship
masteryZone.sol: It concentrated executive and military authority in a single head, pioneering the strong executive model.

masteryZone.q: In which areas did the Governor-General gain absolute authority after the Act of 1786? (Select all that apply)
opts: Direct executive decision-making during emergencies
Supreme command of EIC military forces in India
Abolition of native personal laws
Dissolving the Calcutta Supreme Court
masteryZone.sol: He gained supreme executive veto power and direct military command. Personal laws and Supreme Court were not abolished by this Act.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following are true when the Governor-General overrode his Council under the Act of 1786? (Select all that apply)
opts: He had to issue and sign a formal written order.
He took full personal responsibility for the measures taken.
Dissenting Council members could record their opinions in the official minutes.
Dissenting members were immediately dismissed from office.
masteryZone.sol: The GG had to sign the order, take full responsibility, and council members could record dissents. Dissenters were not dismissed.

masteryZone.q: Which subsequent acts preserved or extended the overriding powers first introduced in 1786? (Select all that apply)
opts: Charter Act of 1793
Charter Act of 1833
Pitts India Act of 1784
Regulating Act of 1773
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1793 extended it to all future GG's and Governors, and the Charter Act of 1833 preserved this centralized power structure.

masteryZone.q: What were the constitutional consequences of combining the offices of GG and Commander-in-Chief? (Select all that apply)
opts: It unified civil-military authority under a single head.
It prevented friction between the army and civil administration.
It subordinated the civil administration to military rule.
It made the Governor-General a direct crown military officer.
masteryZone.sol: It unified civil-military authority and prevented friction, without subordinating civil administration to military rule.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following aspects of the EIC setup remained unchanged by the Amending Act of 1786? (Select all that apply)
opts: The commercial monopoly of the Company
The Double Government system (Board of Control and Court of Directors)
The requirement for the GG to consult his Council
The Governor-General's lack of veto power
masteryZone.sol: The EIC monopoly, Double Government, and consultation requirements remained. The GG's lack of veto power was changed.

masteryZone.q: The override power allowed the Governor-General to ignore his Council in all routine daily commercial decisions.
masteryZone.sol: False. The override power was restricted to special/extraordinary cases concerning safety, peace, or interests.

masteryZone.q: Under the Act of 1786, if the Governor-General overrode his Council, he was required to sign the order personally and take sole responsibility.
masteryZone.sol: True. This ensured absolute personal accountability.

masteryZone.q: Council members lost the right to record their dissenting opinions after the Amending Act of 1786.
masteryZone.sol: False. They could still record their dissents in the Council minutes to be sent to England.

masteryZone.q: The Charter Act of 1793 abolished the overriding power that was introduced in 1786.
masteryZone.sol: False. It extended the overriding power to all future Governor-Generals and Governors.

masteryZone.q: The override power of the Governor-General also applied when the Council sat as the Sadar Diwani Adalat in its judicial capacity.
masteryZone.sol: False. The override power did not apply to judicial judgments.

masteryZone.q: Combining the office of Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief established a precedent of unified civil-military command under a single head.
masteryZone.sol: True. It unified the civil executive and military head in British India.

masteryZone.q: The Board of Control was abolished by the Amending Act of 1786.
masteryZone.sol: False. The Board of Control, created in 1784, was not affected by the 1786 Act.

masteryZone.q: The strong executive model introduced in 1786 influenced subsequent British colonial governance structures in India.
masteryZone.sol: True. It served as a blueprint for executive centralization throughout British rule.

masteryZone.q: The override power of the Governor-General was restricted to matters concerning safety, peace, or ___________.
masteryZone.sol: It applied to matters concerning the safety, peace, or interests of the presidency.

masteryZone.q: When overriding the Council, the Governor-General had to take full ___________ responsibility.
masteryZone.sol: He had to take full personal responsibility and sign the order.

masteryZone.q: Dissenting Council members could record their opinions in the official ___________.
masteryZone.sol: They could record their dissents in the Council minutes.

masteryZone.q: The Charter Act of ___________ extended the overriding power to all future Governor-Generals.
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1793 generalized the override power.

masteryZone.q: The override power did not apply when the GG-in-Council sat in its ___________ capacity.
masteryZone.sol: It did not apply to judicial matters where the Council acted as Sadar Diwani Adalat.

masteryZone.q: The Act of 1786 combined civil executive authority with supreme ___________ command.
masteryZone.sol: It combined the civil executive and military head (Commander-in-Chief).

masteryZone.q: The administrative model introduced in 1786 represents a shift towards a strong ___________ model.
masteryZone.sol: It represents a shift towards a strong executive presidency model.

masteryZone.q: Regulations made by the GG-in-Council were still passed in the name of the Governor-General-in-___________.
masteryZone.sol: Regulations were still passed in the name of the GG-in-Council.

masteryZone.q: Match the statutory features of the Act of 1786 with their constitutional meanings:

options.text: A. GG overrides Council in extraordinary safety/peace cases
B. GG also acts as the Commander-in-Chief of forces
C. Council members register objections in official minutes

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match the scopes of Governor-General's power post-1786:

options.text: A. Subject to override veto in special cases
B. Under direct control of GG as Commander-in-Chief
C. Not subject to override; normal council voting applies

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Match the acts with their long-term constitutional impacts:

options.text: A. Excluded revenue and official acts from Supreme Court
B. Introduced first executive veto for Lord Cornwallis
C. Generalized the veto power to all future Governor-Generals

masteryZone.sol: Options match directly (I-A, II-B, III-C).

masteryZone.q: Under what specific conditions could the Governor-General override his Council?
masteryZone.sol: When he judged the safety, peace, or interests of the British presidency were concerned.

masteryZone.q: What was the Governor-General required to do to execute an override?
masteryZone.sol: He had to sign the order personally and take sole personal responsibility.

masteryZone.q: How could dissenting Council members express their disagreement under the 1786 Act?
masteryZone.sol: By recording their dissents in the official Council minutes.

masteryZone.q: Which act extended the 1786 overriding power to all future Governor-Generals?
masteryZone.sol: The Charter Act of 1793.

masteryZone.q: Did the override power apply to the judicial capacity of the Governor-General-in-Council?
masteryZone.sol: No, it did not apply to judicial matters.

masteryZone.q: What system of governance did the Act of 1786 help pioneer in British India?
masteryZone.sol: The strong executive presidency model.

masteryZone.q: Did the Act of 1786 dissolve the Governor-General's Council?
masteryZone.sol: No, the Council remained and had to be consulted on all matters.

masteryZone.q: Were regulations still passed in the name of the Governor-General-in-Council after 1786?
masteryZone.sol: Yes, regulations were still formally enacted in the name of the GG-in-Council.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The Governor-General could override his Council in routine commercial matters.
Reason (R): The Act of 1786 was designed to maximize EIC commercial trade profits.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are false. The override power was restricted to safety, peace, or interests. It did not cover routine commercial matters.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The Governor-General had to sign overriding orders personally.
Reason (R): This took away his personal liability for the measures.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: A is true. R is false because signing the orders increased his personal accountability, making him solely responsible.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): Dissenting Council members could record their opinions in the official minutes.
Reason (R): This allowed authorities in England to review the executive decisions and check the GG's power.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true, and R is the correct explanation.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The Charter Act of 1793 extended the override power to all future Governor-Generals.
Reason (R): The centralized strong executive model proved highly successful under Cornwallis.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true, and R explains the extension in 1793.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The Governor-General's override veto applied to judicial judgments.
Reason (R): The Governor-General-in-Council sat as the Sadar Diwani Adalat.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: A is false. R is true. The override power did not apply to judicial matters.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The Act of 1786 unified civil and military command in British India.
Reason (R): It allowed the Governor-General to serve as the Commander-in-Chief.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true, and R explains the unification.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The Board of Control's powers were reduced by the Act of 1786.
Reason (R): The Act gave the Governor-General veto power over the Board of Control.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are false. The Board's powers were not reduced, and the GG had no veto over the Board.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The 1786 Act influenced the strong executive presidential model in modern India.
Reason (R): It established a historical precedent of vesting concentrated emergency override powers in a single executive head.
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both are true, and R is the correct explanation.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the override power under the Act of 1786:
1. It allowed the Governor-General to act against the Council's majority vote in special cases.
2. The override power was restricted to safety, peace, or interests of the British territories.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct, describing the mechanism and scope of the veto.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the GG's accountability:
1. The GG had to sign overriding orders himself, taking sole responsibility.
2. Council members could veto the GG's override by unanimous vote.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because the Council could not veto the GG's override.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Charter Act of 1793:
1. It abolished the overriding veto power introduced in 1786.
2. It extended the overriding power to all future Governor-Generals and Presidency Governors.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is incorrect because it extended rather than abolished the power.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the office of Commander-in-Chief:
1. It was combined with the Governor-Generalship for Lord Cornwallis.
2. The combination was meant to ensure unified civil-military command.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are correct.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the legislative rules post-1786:
1. Regulations were still enacted in the name of the Governor-General-in-Council.
2. The override power could be used to pass judicial appeals in the Sadar Diwani Adalat.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
opts: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
masteryZone.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because the override veto was not applicable to judicial capacities.

masteryZone.q: Why was the Governor-General's override veto power restricted to safety, peace, or interests?
masteryZone.sol: To ensure it was only used for major emergency and security matters, preserving collective Council decision-making for routine commercial and administrative affairs.

masteryZone.q: Why was the Governor-General required to sign overriding orders personally?
masteryZone.sol: To ensure absolute accountability and prevent him from deflecting responsibility onto the Council members for measures taken against their consensus.

masteryZone.q: Why did the Charter Act of 1793 extend the override power to all future Governor-Generals?
masteryZone.sol: Because the centralized strong executive model proved highly successful under Cornwallis, facilitating stable governance and military campaigns, prompting Parliament to make it permanent.

masteryZone.q: How did the override power affect the balance of power between the Governor-General and his Council?
masteryZone.sol: It shifted the balance heavily in favor of the Governor-General, transitioning the executive from a collective committee (where the GG had only one vote) to a strong centralized executive presidency.

masteryZone.q: How did Council members record their dissents when overridden?
masteryZone.sol: They recorded their opinions and dissents in the official Council minutes, which were sent to the Court of Directors in London for oversight.

masteryZone.q: How did the Act of 1786 influence the modern Indian constitutional structure?
masteryZone.sol: It established the historical precedent of vesting concentrated emergency override and executive powers in a single head of state (precursor to presidential emergency and override powers).

masteryZone.q: Case Study: During the Third Anglo-Mysore War, Lord Cornwallis personally took command of the military forces and made executive decisions on treaties. How did the Act of 1786 facilitate this?
masteryZone.sol: By combining the offices of Governor-General and Commander-in-Chief and granting override powers, the Act allowed him to lead campaigns with full civil backing and without council friction.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: In a hypothetical scenario, a Governor-General in 1788 wants to override his Council on a tax rate dispute. Would the override power under the 1786 Act apply here?
masteryZone.sol: Only if the tax rate dispute directly threatened the safety, peace, or interests of the presidency. For routine tax administration, he had to work through normal council consensus.

masteryZone.q: Case Study: The Charter Act of 1793 extended the override power to all future Governor-Generals. What does this suggest about the EIC's administration after Cornwallis?
masteryZone.sol: It suggests that the centralized strong executive system was deemed highly successful and necessary to manage a growing colonial empire in India.

masteryZone.q: Explain how the override veto power worked under the Amending Act of 1786.
masteryZone.sol: In special cases concerning safety or peace, the GG could override the majority council vote. He had to sign the order personally and take sole responsibility, while councilors recorded their dissents in the minutes.

masteryZone.q: Explain why the override power did not apply to judicial matters.
masteryZone.sol: Because judicial matters involved appellate courts (Sadar Diwani Adalat) which required following established legal protocols and native personal laws, where executive veto was deemed inappropriate and a violation of basic legal norms.

masteryZone.q: Explain the long-term constitutional legacy of the Amending Act of 1786.
masteryZone.sol: It established the precedent of a strong, centralized executive head in India, which was extended by the Charter Act of 1793 and survived throughout British rule, later influencing the strong executive and emergency frameworks in modern India's Constitution.
